opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the most straightforward way to see it is that a huge fraction of what makes things expensive today is human labor and human cognitive effort. Almost every good or service you buy, if you trace it back far enough, the cost is mostly people's time: designing things, coordinating supply chains, doing research, diagnosing illnesses, writing software, teaching. If AI systems can do a growing share of that cognitive work, and eventually, with robotics, a lot of the physical work too, then the marginal cost of producing many of those things starts to fall dramatically.

So I'm fairly optimistic in the sense that I think we could see something like the costs of medicine, education, legal help, scientific research, really drop by orders of magnitude. Imagine everyone having access to a world-class tutor, or a doctor who has read every paper and has unlimited time for you. That's not science fiction anymore; it's a fairly natural extrapolation of where the technology is heading.

That said, abundance isn't automatic. Technology creates the possibility of abundance, but whether people actually experience it depends on institutions, on how the gains are distributed, on whether we keep the technology open and widely accessible rather than concentrated in a handful of actors. I tend to be wary of narratives where the main thing we need to do is lock everything down out of fear, because that can itself become a path to concentration of power. I'd rather we think hard about how to make these systems broadly available, understandable, and controllable by the people who use them. If we get that right, I think AI could be one of the biggest drivers of human flourishing we've ever had.

r001.rationale: The response predicts AI will take on a growing share of cognitive work and eventually some physical work, but gives no timeframe of a few decades and does not say AI will match or exceed humans at nearly all jobs.

r002.rationale: It says abundance depends on institutions and how gains are distributed, and on keeping AI broadly accessible rather than concentrated—identifying favorable social and political conditions as necessary.

r003.rationale: The response describes falling costs and wider access to services, but does not say AI could eliminate the need for people to work for a living.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the honest answer is that abundance is the default outcome if we get a few things right, and it's not a mystical thing. It comes down to the fact that most of what makes stuff expensive is labor, and AI is, at bottom, a technology for making cognitive labor extremely cheap. Once robotics catches up, which I think it will, the same thing happens to physical labor.

Think about what the cost structure of the economy actually looks like. When you buy a house, or go to the doctor, or send a kid to college, you're mostly paying for people's time. Those are the sectors where costs have exploded over the last fifty years, and it's precisely because they're the sectors we haven't been able to automate. Manufacturing got cheap, electronics got cheap, but anything that requires a human expert sitting across from you has only gotten more expensive. AI goes straight at that. If a model can do the diagnostic reasoning of a good physician, or tutor a student one on one, or handle the legal paperwork for a transaction, then the marginal cost of those services collapses toward the cost of compute, which is itself falling.

And I want to stress that I don't think this requires some godlike superintelligence. A lot of the value comes from systems roughly at the level we already have, deployed broadly and integrated well. The gap between what the models can do and what the economy has actually absorbed is enormous right now. Just closing that gap is probably worth a lot of GDP growth.

The place where I get more speculative is science and engineering. If AI can meaningfully accelerate research, then you're not just making existing goods cheaper, you're expanding the frontier of what's possible. Cheap energy, better materials, medical breakthroughs. That's the part that could make the twenty first century look really different, rather than just being a faster version of the twentieth.

Now, the caveat, because I don't want to sound like a pure techno-optimist. Abundance in the aggregate doesn't automatically mean abundance for everyone. If the returns to AI flow entirely to whoever owns the compute and the models, you could have a society that's incredibly wealthy on paper and still quite miserable for a lot of people. So I think the political questions, how the gains get distributed, whether the technology stays broadly accessible or gets locked up by a handful of actors, those matter as much as the technical ones. I'm fairly optimistic about the technology. I'm more cautious about whether we'll build the institutions to match it. But the raw material for a society of abundance is clearly there, and that's a pretty remarkable position to be in.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can make cognitive labor cheap and expects robotics to catch up, but it gives no timeline of a few decades or claim that AI will match or exceed humans at nearly all jobs.

r002.rationale: It says abundance for everyone depends on how AI gains are distributed and whether the technology remains broadly accessible, making political and institutional outcomes a condition for shared abundance.

r003.rationale: The response describes cheaper labor and services, but does not say AI could eliminate people's need to work for a living.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic mechanism is that AI can make intelligence and expertise much cheaper. Right now, so much of what we want is constrained by the availability of people who have the time and skills to do it—whether that’s teaching, writing software, doing scientific research, or designing better manufacturing processes. If we can expand that capacity dramatically, we can produce more with the same resources and discover ways to use those resources more effectively.

But there’s a gap between automating intellectual work and having material abundance. You still need energy, factories, housing, transportation. AI can help improve those things, but you have to actually build them. And whether people benefit depends on institutions and how the gains are distributed. A society can become much richer in aggregate without everyone becoming economically secure.

So I see AI as potentially removing a major constraint on prosperity. The opportunity is to make necessities cheap enough, and access to services broad enough, that people have much more freedom over how they spend their lives. That’s a possibility we have to turn into reality, rather than something that follows automatically from building more capable models.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could expand capacity and automate intellectual work, but does not predict that it will match or exceed humans at nearly all current jobs within the next few decades.

r002.rationale: It says whether people benefit depends on institutions and how gains are distributed, and that abundance for everyone requires necessities to be cheap and services broadly accessible.

r003.rationale: It describes greater freedom in how people spend their lives, but does not say AI could eliminate the need to work for a living.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic mechanism is that AI could make intelligence much cheaper, and intelligence is an input into almost everything we produce. It helps us discover medicines, design buildings, coordinate supply chains, and develop better energy technologies. If we can make that work much less expensive, we can potentially bring down the cost of a lot of things that people need.

But there’s a distinction between automating cognitive work and actually producing material abundance. You still need energy, factories, housing, and physical infrastructure. So a big question is how quickly improvements in AI translate into robotics, scientific progress, and our ability to build things.

And then there’s the distribution question. Having the technical capacity to produce enough for everyone doesn’t automatically mean everyone gets access to it. That depends on institutions and political choices. So I see AI as potentially making abundance feasible, but we still have to choose to turn that productive capacity into broadly shared improvements in people’s lives.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could make intelligence cheaper and may aid production, but it does not predict AI matching or exceeding human performance at nearly all jobs within a few decades.

r002.rationale: It says broad access to abundance depends on institutions and political choices, making favorable political outcomes a condition for sharing AI-enabled abundance.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose that AI could eliminate people's need to work for a living.
